## Today's Learning Goals

By the end of class, you should be able to:

- Set up Codex and understand your access options.
- Improve prompts to answer a marketing question with R summaries and charts.
- Use explanations and feedback to build your understanding.
- Check campaign comparisons and AI conclusions, and try a plugin.
- Use the Lecture Setup Skill to organize materials from Canvas.

## Simple Tasks

Codex is an AI agent that can work with files and programs on your computer.

| When you need help with... | A useful request |
|---|---|
| Understanding Code | "Explain what each line of this code does." |
| Fixing an Error | "Explain this error and suggest the simplest fix." |
| Choosing a Function | "Which tidyverse function should I use to keep only Email orders?" |
| Making a Plot | "Help me make a bar chart of revenue by marketing channel." |

You supply the prompt and evaluate the result.

## Complex Tasks {.complex-tasks}

| When you need help with... | A useful request |
|---|---|
| Brainstorming | "My client wants to identify the most valuable customers. I think we should start by identifying who made the most recent purchases. Can you identify any shortcomings with this approach, and suggest alternative definitions of 'valuable' customers? Then we'll identify the pros and cons of each definition together." |
| Vibe Coding | "Based on this analysis of most valuable customers, I want to build a dashboard that allows decision makers to easily query the data and visualize customer characteristics. Let's start by outlining an implementation plan and then executing on that plan. I'll rely on you to write the back end code, so please provide me with a way to access the front-end dashboard to evaluate it and provide feedback." |

## Your First Project

1. Download **`hillstrom-practice.zip` from the Codex lecture on Canvas**.

| Part of the app | What you do there |
|---|---|
| Project and task list | Navigate your folders and conversations. |
| Message box | Name a file, describe a goal, and give follow-up instructions. |
| File or change view | Open the saved output and inspect edits. |

## Saving Files Before Codex Makes Changes

- SAVE YOUR WORK **BEFORE** PROMPTING CODEX.
- Codex works with the saved file on your hard drive. 
- If you have unsaved edits, they exist only in RStudio.
- If Codex makes changes to an unsaved file, you can lose your unsaved edits. 
- Saving your copy after Codex makes changes can overwrite Codex's changes.
- **Let's see an example of what NOT to do...**

## The Hillstrom Campaign Decision

A retailer wants to generate sales using an email campaign.

**Given the data, which email, if either, should it repeat? What evidence supports that choice?**

The data contain 64,000 customers randomly assigned to:

- An email featuring men's merchandise.
- An email featuring women's merchandise.
- No email.

We observe purchases and spending over the following **two weeks**.

**Discuss:** How would we determine whether a campaign should be repeated?

<!-- Instructor: Allow students to propose measures before revealing a solution.
We are assessing short-term revenue for a similar audience. We cannot establish
profitability without costs and margins. No predictive model is needed.
See instructor/hillstrom-teaching-guide.md for timing and verified results. -->

## Our First Prompt

> Add code to make a bar chart comparing average spend among customers who purchased in the two email campaigns.

Run the prompt and inspect the saved code and chart.

- Which campaign looks better by this measure?
- What does this plot not account for?
- Does this answer the retailer's business question?

<!-- Instructor: This is a deliberately incomplete analytical request, not an
instruction for Codex to make an error. Purchasers' two-week spending averages
$113.53 for men's email and $121.89 for women's email. These are not average
order values: customers, not orders, are the unit of observation.
Codex may flag the limitation immediately. Acknowledge that success and have
students explain it. Do not force or claim an incorrect live response. -->

## Add A Clearer Goal and Relevant Context

**Prompting tip:** Explain the decision and ask for clarification.

> Our goal is to establish whether an email campaign increased revenue. 
> Does our first chart answer that question?
> Explain any mismatch and ask us one question about how to measure
> success before changing the analysis.

Does AI identify any key issues?

<p class="source"><a href="https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering">OpenAI: clear instructions and relevant context</a>.</p>

<!-- Instructor: Have students supply their own definition first. A useful
resolution is two-week revenue per assigned customer, compared with no email.
The next slide gives an output example after that discussion. If students
choose another metric, compare its business implications explicitly. -->

## A More Useful Deliverable

**Prompting tip:** Refine the goal, specify the desired output and define an example of its structure.

(Adapt the following as needed):

> Revise demo.qmd to answer our business question using numerical summaries and a chart.
> Include all email campaign groups (including no email). The numerical summaries should be
> contained in a table with one row per group. Include customer counts, purchase rate, and revenue per targeted customer. 
Keep the raw data unchanged. Use readable tidyverse code.

**Example table headings:**

Group / Customers / Purchase rate / Revenue per customer

<!-- Instructor: These are deliverable requirements, not a prescribed sequence
of R operations. Students and Codex decide how to implement them. Ask students
what the denominator is before running. Use unrounded values for differences.
A bar chart of group means is enough. Do not add predictive modeling. -->

## Specific Feedback on the Output

**Prompting tip:** Name the problem you actually observe.

Compare the revised output with your first chart.

- Are the units and the two-week period clear?
- Can a reader identify the comparison group?
- Does the written recommendation follow from the numbers?

> We need to make the following improvements....
> Make those changes and explain back to me how the change helps answer our business question.
> Make sure to preserve the portions of the analysis that are already correct.

**Class contribution:** Agree on one specific piece of feedback before sending it.

<!-- Instructor: Do not invent a defect if the output is already strong.
Examples, only if needed: ambiguous dollars-per-person labels, excessive
decimal places, a missing no-email row, or an explanation that mistakes
revenue per purchaser for revenue per assigned customer. -->

## Honest Conclusions

**Prompting tip:** Supply evidence and invite disagreement.

> The analysis so far suggests that the Men's merchandise email raised revenue per customer significantly
> compared to the no email group. We could recommend that campaign to the client, but does the 
> evidence support that that campaign truly increases revenue? Give a critical evaluation, and state
> any additional evidence we need to give a strong recommendation.

<p class="source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798">Huang et al. (2024): limits of self-correction without external feedback</a>.</p>

<!-- Instructor: External reference: men's email $30,311.69 / 21,307 customers
= $1.422616511. No email: $13,908.33 / 21,306 = $0.652789355. Difference:
$0.769827156 per assigned customer. Do not demand artificial certainty.
Random assignment supports the comparison, but this class activity has not
quantified sampling uncertainty. Historical results do not guarantee future
results, and campaign costs/margins are absent. The cited paper studied
particular earlier models/tasks; it does not guarantee current Codex behavior. -->

## Revision and Simplification

**Prompting tip:** Ask for a focused revision.

> Review demo.qmd and remove non-essential complexity. Keep the summaries,
> chart, and checks needed for our business question. Use readable
> tidyverse code. Explain each change and
> rerun the R code chunks to verify that the numerical results stay the same.

**Review together:**

- Which change makes the analysis easier to understand?
- Did we accidentally lose an important check or limitation?
- If the work was already simple, was any change necessary?

<p class="source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651">Madaan et al., Self-Refine (2023)</a>. The simplification phrase is course guidance, not a guarantee of improvement.</p>

## Our Recommendation to the Retailer

Write your own answer first, then ask Codex for a concise revision.

> I've written a short recommendation in the .qmd file. Revise it to be more professional
> and ensure that I am not making claims that the data don't support. Use only results we have checked together.

Compare that answer with your initial recommendation.

**Discuss:** Which improvement to the prompt changed the business answer most?
Which change only improved how we communicated it?

## Learning with Codex

Choose the kind of help you need:

> "Give me one hint about why including nonbuyers changes our campaign comparison."

> "Explain what `|>` does in our Hillstrom code. Use one calculation to illustrate it."

> "Quiz me on inner joins vs. left joins, one question at a time. Once I
> consistently answer your questions correctly, give me three hypothetical
> join scenarios, where I need to determine which type of join to use."

> "Here is my explanation of the code. What did I misunderstand?"

## Checking AI Work

**Ask AI to track the exact lines it changes and report back on those changes!**

- **Review:** Read the changed lines and ask what each change accomplishes
  if it isn't apparent.
- **Run:** Run the R code chunks in the saved document in RStudio. Check errors and output.
- **Verify:** Do calculations by hand, or ask for a different method to verify
  the result.
- **Interpret:** Does our campaign comparison answer the business question?

**Remember**: You are responsible for understanding the work you submit.

## Plugins, Skills, and Connectors

| Component | What it does | Two examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Plugin** | An installable package that adds capabilities, such as skills or connections to tools. | **Spreadsheets:** work with Excel files.<br>**Chrome:** work in your browser. |
| **Skill** | Reusable instructions and resources for a particular task or workflow. | **Lecture Setup:** organize Canvas materials.<br>**OpenAI Docs:** consult official product documentation. |
| **Connector** | A connection that lets Codex read information or take authorized actions in an external service. | **Google Drive:** access shared documents.<br>**GitHub:** access code repositories. |

A plugin can include skills, connectors, or both.

<p class="source"><a href="https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/plugins">Official plugin, skill, and connector definitions</a>. Checked September 9, 2026.</p>

## A Reusable Skill: Lecture Setup

The browser plugin provides access. A **skill** supplies a repeatable workflow.

1. Download [lecture-setup.zip](lecture-setup.zip) with this lecture's materials
   and extract the `lecture-setup` folder into your course folder.
2. Open that local folder in Codex and ask:

> "Install the `lecture-setup` folder as a personal Codex skill.

The skill identifies the lecture, downloads student materials, and places
them in the corresponding local folder while preserving your existing work.

## Five-Minute Practice

The retailer now asks whether **website visits** tell the same story as revenue.

Using the same Hillstrom data, work with a partner to request a compact
comparison of all three groups and a brief answer. Keep demo.qmd's revenue
analysis available for comparison.

- Decide what a fair comparison of visits would show.
- Write a prompt that names the goal, context, and desired output.
- Check one result independently, then give Codex specific feedback.
- Explain whether your finding changes the recommendation and why.

Be ready to share one prompt improvement and one check you performed.
